This technique entails putting tissue in the freezer overnight and collecting cells early the next morning. Because normal cells have increased methylation levels in comparison to the abnormal cells, fluorescence in situ hybridisation can spot the changes in the tissue.

The energy of those X-rays emitted from Uranus appears to come primarily from a long-lived magnetic field just above the planet's sulfur oceans. Very little of that energy actually extends outward to Uranus's core. NASA's Voyager spacecraft measured an unusual magnetic field in the middle of Uranus in the 1980s. Telescopes on other planets already spotted this magnetic field, but Uranus' was the first time an outer planet was measured to have a similar magnetic field to Earth. With a strong magnetic field, plasma heats up more easily. Uranus in turn will produce an abundance of X-rays that edge out the lower temperature of the gas. That results in a particle wind, which is an outflow of particles from an animated source. Because Uranus has a faster jet stream, more particles are ejected from the planet in the magnetic field. So more particles mean more X-rays.
